texts: my child, my own
My son leaves for college tomorrow and I keep finding reasons to ask him to stay one more week, though I know it is not fair to him.
doha about not being able to let go of the people we call mine
Please write a doha about how the little word mine ties the heart to a wife, a child, a family, so that every parting becomes a wound and every loss a grief that we cannot let go of.
Mine, mine, cries the heart, and the word is a bond that no eye can see yet every heart can feel.
Every day I cross the bridge to visit my aging mother and I cannot bear the thought of a world without her, though I know she herself wants me to let go. Please write a doha about this attachment.
doha with a bridge, about not being able to let go of my family
Across the bridge the mother waits, across the bridge the child returns, and the heart that calls them mine is bound to both banks.
My daughter's wedding is next month and I keep crossing the bridge to her new home just to see her face one more time.
bridge, mother's attachment
The grindstone grinds the grain and the sword cuts the cord, yet the love that says mine is not ground or cut.
grindstone, sword, attachment
My brother says he is brave as a sword, but when his son cries he is ground down like grain on a grindstone, and cannot bear to be apart from him.
Write a doha where neither the grindstone nor the sword can cut or grind the bond of a father who calls his child mine, showing how deep the hook of attachment goes into the human heart.
doha with a grindstone and a sword, about being too attached to my kids
The heron stands guard over the fish it calls its own, and the heart stands guard over the loved ones it calls mine.
doha with a heron and a fish, about being too attached to my family
I watched a heron stand over a fish for ages, unable to leave it, and I thought of how I stay up every night waiting for my teenage son to come home.
heron, fish, protective attachment
Please write a doha where a heron guards a single fish as though it were its own treasure, to show the way we cling to people and things we call mine, and cannot bear to have them out of sight.
mine, mine, mine
Sweet is the word mine when spoken, and bitter the grief when what is called mine is taken away.
I would like a doha about how a parent suffers because the heart insists on calling a child my own, and how this very claim makes every farewell heavier than it needs to be.
When my youngest got his own flat across town, I stood in his empty room for an hour, unable to go back downstairs.
doha on being too attached to my own people
doha about how hard it is to let go of my kids even when they grow up
My wife can't sleep until our grown-up daughter texts that she has reached her hostel, and I'm the same, and it is slowly wearing us both down.
unable to let go
What the heart calls mine it holds till it aches, and when it must let go, it breaks.

Please write a doha about how the love of parents turns into a hook that will not release, so that even when the child is grown the parent still claims him as mine and suffers each time he walks away.
need a doha on being attached to my family so much it hurts
attachment to my own

Write a doha about the quiet pain of a person who loves so tightly that he cannot bear any distance from his wife and children, as though the word mine grew tighter around his heart with every farewell.
Love that says mine is half love and half bondage, and the bondage is the part that hurts.
When my husband went abroad for work, I cried at the airport like a child, though we had both agreed it was for the best.
doha with a chakor bird, about being too attached to someone you cant have
The chakor bird gazes at the one it calls its own, and cannot look away even when it is told the gaze is a chain.
My cousin keeps staring at his ex's pictures like a chakor bird at the sky, and cannot move on though the whole family tells him to.
Write a doha where a chakor bird, locked in longing for the one it calls mine, cannot turn away even when the beloved has gone, to show how attachment to a particular person ties the heart.
chakor bird, attachment
The snake guards its hole, the thief eyes it, and the heart that calls things mine fears both.
snake, thief, my possessions
Write a doha where a snake coils around what it calls its own and a thief circles for a chance, to show how the hook of mine makes us guard anxiously whatever we love and call ours.
doha with a snake and a thief, about being too attached to my stuff
After a thief stole my bike I was angrier than I had any right to be, and then I saw I was guarding every little thing I owned like a snake.
needle, attachment
doha with a needle, about being attached to someone like a stitch to cloth
My grandmother kept her husband's old needle and sewing box for forty years after he passed, and never once let anyone move it.
The needle pierces the cloth and drags its binding behind, and so mine pierces the heart and drags its loves behind.

Please write a doha where a needle pulls a stitch through cloth, binding two pieces together, to show how the word mine pulls the heart through every person and thing it holds close and cannot release.
The oil press crushes the grain and still the sand holds on to what it has swallowed, as the heart holds to what it calls mine.
oil press, sand, clinging heart
My father kept his old oil press running long after it made no profit, and when I asked him to sell it, he said he'd sooner sell me.
doha with an oil press and sand, about being attached to my old stuff
Write a doha where an oil press that has served for years is tied to its owner's heart, like sand that clings to every hand it touches, showing how attachment to what is mine outlasts all reason.
elephant, mine
Our elephant at the village festival stood held by a tiny cord, and I realised my own attachment to my kids is just as thin yet equally unbreakable.
The elephant is held by a thin cord, though it could snap it with a breath, for the memory of mine holds it.
Write a doha where a great elephant is held by the thinnest cord, not because it cannot break free but because its heart is bound to the post it calls home, as we are bound to what we call mine.
doha with an elephant, about being so attached to someone you cant move on
Weeping at the departure, laughing at the return, the heart that says mine lives and dies a hundred times a day.
doha about the pain of loving people so much that you cant let them go
I want a doha about the suffering a mother feels when her child goes out into the world, and about how her love, though pure, also holds on with a hook that causes both of them pain.
love that will not release
Every time my daughter leaves for school I follow her to the corner, though she is fifteen and asks me not to.
doha with a house and an inn, how my attachment to my home hurts
Please write a doha about the difference between a house we call mine and an inn we stay in for a night, to show that the pain of attachment comes only from the first, because it claims ownership.
house, inn, mine
When we sold our family house I cried more than at some funerals, while at the inn on holiday I left without a glance back.
The inn is left at dawn without a tear, the house is wept over for years, for only one is called mine.
The sword cuts the cord of birth and death, but never the cord that says mine, which binds the father to the son.
doha with a sword, about being too attached to my kids and family
sword, parental attachment
I know all the philosophy about letting go, but when my son goes out in the night with a sharp worry in my chest, it all vanishes.
Write a doha where the sword of reason can cut many things but is blunted by the one cord, a parent's love for a child called mine, which no blade can sever and no wisdom can easily loosen.
doha with the sun, about not wanting to let my kids go even though they grow up
Each evening I watch the sun set behind my parents' old home and cannot imagine a day when I will no longer visit them there.
The sun sets on the home that is called mine, and the heart weeps, as though the sun belonged to the heart.
sun, my own home
Please write a doha where the sun rises and sets over a home that a family calls its own, and each setting is felt as a small death by those who claim every person in it as mine.
Please write a doha about how a man who is never sad about strangers dying weeps for his own child's small illness, showing how the hook of mine makes our suffering depend on whom we claim.
Strangers may fall and the heart sleeps on, but when mine is hurt, the world ends.
When the news said fifty people had died in a flood I felt a little sad, but when my son had a mild fever I couldn't sleep or eat for two days.
grief for mine alone
doha about how we only really care about people we call our own
The fly clings to sand, the heart to its kin, and both are caught by what they will not leave.
Write a doha where a fly clings to sticky sand and cannot fly away, just as the heart clings to those it calls its own, and cannot rise into freedom as long as the claim of mine is strong.
doha with a fly and sand, about being stuck on someone because of attachment
fly, sand, stuck
A fly kept dragging its wings through the damp sand at the beach, and I thought of my ex and how I cannot pull myself free.
doha about being too attached to a person, cant let go
my own, my own
Where there is mine there is tears, and where there is no mine there is no weeping.
Please write a doha about the grandmother who still cooks her grandson's favourite dish every day though he has moved to another city, and about the pain of a love that clings to a name.
My father still keeps my childhood bed made up, even though I live abroad and come once in two years.
My mother counts her prayer beads each morning with her eyes on the phone, waiting for her daughter to call, and no bead brings her peace until she hears that voice.
Write a doha where a woman tells her prayer beads while her ears strain for the cuckoo's call that reminds her of her far-off son, showing how mine pulls the heart even in prayer.
doha with prayer beads and a cuckoo, about being too attached to my family while praying
The beads slip through the fingers but the heart slips to the child, and the cuckoo's cry is the name it calls.
prayer beads, cuckoo, longing
I get irrationally upset when my brother uses my things without asking, even when I know I don't even need them.
the hook of mine
I want a doha about the small stab of loss a person feels when someone borrows what is his, and how it is the same feeling that makes us grieve for the people we love and call our own.
doha about being possessive over my stuff
Mine is the word that builds a wall around the heart, and the wall is a prison for the one who built it.

Please write a doha about the parent who cannot attend a wedding without sobbing, who loves his children so much that every milestone feels like a loss, and who needs to learn that mine is the hook, not love.
doha about being unable to let go of my loved ones
At my sister's wedding my father cried more than anyone, and not from joy; he kept saying she'd always been his and now was not.
He gave away his daughter and wept, as though a gift had ever been his to give.
loved ones as mine

A soldier with a sword in his hand fears no battle but trembles when he thinks of his child at home, for that thought alone cuts deeper than any blade. Please write a doha about the hook of attachment.
My uncle, who served in the army for twenty years, tears up at the gate whenever his grandson leaves after a visit, as if the old sword were still in his hand and could not help.
doha with a sword, about a brave person weak with love for his family
sword, a father's fear
The sword fears nothing, yet its master quakes at the name of his child; such is the hook of mine.
mine, therefore pain
I'd like a doha about the way we cling to a marriage, a job, a title, even a favourite chair as mine, and how the pain we feel at losing them is the price of the word.
When my colleague got my corner desk after a reorganisation I was surprisingly heartbroken, as if a piece of me had been taken.
Wherever the heart plants the word mine, it grows a sorrow that stings the planter.
doha about being too possessive of the things and people in my life
Alchemists seek the philosopher's stone to turn all to riches, yet the word mine, in a mother's heart, turns a child into the entire world and every parting into grief. Please write a doha for that.
doha with a philosopher's stone, about how loving someone as mine turns to pain
philosopher's stone, my child
The philosopher's stone turns lead to wealth, but the word mine turns love into bondage.
My friend hunted for years for a perfect cure to fix his dying father, as though some philosopher's stone existed, because he could not bear to say goodbye.
At the cremation ground I watched a man cling to his father's body and refuse to leave, while an old man nearby ate a bitter gourd calmly, and I thought about how mine hurts.
doha with a cremation ground and a bitter gourd, about the pain of attachment
Write a doha where a man at the cremation ground cries over what he called mine, and a plain bitter gourd on the wall reminds the watcher that attachment is the bitterness at the root of all grief.
At the cremation ground the weeper learns that mine was only a word, and bitter is the gourd of that learning.
cremation ground, bitter gourd, attachment
fire, cremation ground, mine
The fire at the cremation ground takes what the heart calls mine, and the heart is burned along with it.
When we lit the pyre at the cremation ground for my brother, I could feel my own heart burn, because I had claimed him as mine for forty years.
doha with a fire and a cremation ground, about how attachment hurts when we lose someone
Write a doha where the fire at the cremation ground consumes the body of a loved one, and the mourner learns that the pain is born of the word mine, which the fire cannot burn.
Say not my son, my wife, my own, for the word wounds the one who speaks it.
Please write a doha for a family at a long goodbye, where everyone is weeping and holding on, and where an older voice gently points out that the hook of mine is what makes parting so heavy.
doha about letting go of the people we love
dropping the word mine
My daughter was so tired of my calling her my baby that she once said, mum, I'm not yours, I'm mine, and I am still thinking about it.
Jaggery is sweet and sticks to the fingers, and the furnace is hot and burns the one who lingers near, like the love of a mother that clings and burns. Please write a doha on the hook of mine.
doha with jaggery and a furnace, about attachment that is sweet but burns
Sweet as jaggery is the word mine, and hot as the furnace is the grief that follows it.
My grandmother made jaggery sweets for us every winter by the furnace in her yard, and could not bear it when we left; I'd love a doha on this.
jaggery, furnace, mine
A bird in a cage is kept by a loving owner who cannot bear to let it go, though the furnace of grief burns him when it sulks; please write a doha on how attachment makes a cage of love.
Love built a cage and called it home, and the furnace of grief was lit to keep it warm.
doha with a cage and a furnace, about attachment that traps the people we love
cage, furnace, possessive love
My mother-in-law keeps her only son so close that he stays in her cage of worry, and she suffers a furnace of fear when he is out of her sight.
beggar, mine
doha with a beggar, about how even a poor man clings to what is his
A beggar at our corner has refused all offers of help because he cannot leave his spot, and I understood that I too am tied to my things.
A beggar outside the shrine clutches a tattered bundle as if it were a treasure, and a king clings to his throne in the same way; write a doha on how mine binds the poor and the rich alike.
The beggar clutches his rags and the king his crown, and both are held by the same hook.
The mind says release and the heart says hold, and the one word between them is mine.
I would like a doha about the parent who lies awake wondering whether the child is safe, who cannot rest unless he knows where the child is, and who calls this love when it is also the hook of mine.
Even now that my son is thirty, I wait for his message that he has reached home safely, and I feel the anxiety rising whenever he is late.
possessive worry
doha for a mom who cant stop worrying about her kids
doha about being too attached to my belongings
I have a cupboard of old toys from my kids' childhood and I refuse to give away a single one, though they haven't been touched in twenty years.
my things, my people
Please write a doha about how a person who holds on to every object and every person as mine suffers when anything is lost, and how freedom begins only when the claim is loosened.
Whatever is mine becomes a master, and the one who claimed it becomes a servant to its loss.
doha on the pain of attachment to kids and family
Please write a doha about the way a woman's world shrinks to the small circle of those she calls hers, so that all her joy and fear depends on them, and the hook of mine becomes a prison.
After my kids moved out I walked through the empty rooms every day for months, touching their things, unable to accept that the home was only mine now.
love as a hook
The heart that draws a boundary around its own is a prisoner inside its own love.
grindstone, attachment
The old grindstone in my mother's kitchen belonged to her mother and she refuses to part with it, though it takes up half the room and nobody uses it.
The grindstone is worn by years of grinding and the heart is worn by the years of calling things mine.
doha with a grindstone, about being attached to old family things
Write a doha where a grindstone inherited from a mother is held on to by a daughter long after its use is gone, showing how the hook of mine makes us hold family objects as if they were the family.
Mine is the bond that ties the heart to a thousand loves, and every bond is a fresh grief waiting.

I'd like a doha about how we are born alone and will die alone, yet spend a lifetime clinging to wives, husbands, children and friends as if they belonged to us, and suffer when they inevitably leave.
At 60 I realised the greatest pain of my life has always come from loving a few people as if they were mine to keep.
doha about how loving people as mine makes losing them hurt
possessive love
The mother says my child, the father says my son, and neither knows the child belongs to the life that sent him.
Please write a doha for new parents who feel a sudden fierce hold on their baby, helping them see that love need not be a possession, and that the hook of mine is the cause of future grief.
Since the baby was born I cannot be in a different room even for ten minutes, and my husband says I'll make us both ill with worry.
my baby, mine
doha about parental attachment that gets too intense
doha with a physician and cotton, about being too attached to a sick family member
The physician told me to rest, but I sat beside my mother's bed with a cotton cloth on her forehead all night, unable to bear the thought of leaving her.
The physician's art can heal the body, but the heart's hook of mine needs a medicine he cannot give, and the cotton is soaked in tears.
physician, cotton, my beloved
Write a doha where a physician speaks of recovery but the wife sits beside her husband with cotton on his brow, unable to eat or sleep, because her heart's hook of mine will not let her rest.
My neighbour clings to his shop and his savings like sand to wet fingers, and when a fire broke out last winter he rushed into it to save just one old trunk.
Sand clings to the hand that tries to brush it off, and so mine clings to the heart in the fire of loss.
doha with sand and fire, about attachment to my things
Write a doha where sand clings to a man's hand and a fire threatens his belongings, and he runs to save what he calls his own, showing how the hook of mine makes us risk everything for things.
sand, fire, possessiveness
sword, mountain, attachment
doha with a sword and a mountain, about being so attached that nothing helps
The sword is strong and the mountain is high, but the hook of mine goes deeper than either.
Write a doha where a warrior climbs a mountain with his sword to escape the world, yet carries in his heart a child called mine, and finds that no height or blade can free him from that hook.
My brother went on a mountain trek to clear his mind, but he spent the whole trip phoning his wife and son every hour, sword-sharp with worry.
crossroads, mine
doha with a crossroads, about not being able to let go of the people you love
At a crossroads a father watches his son walk away on the other road and cannot make himself turn back, because the hook of mine is stronger than the wisdom to let him go. Please write a doha.
At the crossroads each goes his own way, but the hook of mine tugs the heart in both directions.
When my daughter chose the other road at the crossroads of her life and moved cities, I stayed at the bus stop for an hour after she left.
doha about the pain of loving people as if they belong to us
What the heart calls mine it protects with tears, and what it protects with tears it cannot release without pain.
When my parents sold their old home I cried for a week, not because I had lived there recently but because I had always considered it mine.
Please write a doha about the way a person who builds his life around his family finds it unbearable to see any of them change, move, or leave, and how the claim of mine is the source of the hurt.
attachment, grief
The heart that holds too closely is wounded by its own hold, and calls the wound love.
doha about not wanting to let go of someone
My sister still sets a place for her late husband at the table every evening, and no one in the family dares say a word.
Write a doha for the mother who tells herself she is only protecting her grown children when she is actually holding them back, so that her love and her fear of loss have become indistinguishable.
love that grips
doha about my attachment to my kids and what it does to me
Please write a doha about how a heart that calls so many people and things mine is divided into a hundred pieces, each of which can be broken, and how few notice until the first loss comes.
I realised at my father's funeral that half my sadness was not for him but for the part of my own life that was ending along with him.
hook of mine
A heart that says mine a hundred times is wounded a hundred times.
my children, my pain
doha on the heartache of loving children too possessively
Please write a doha about the parent who sacrifices everything for a child and then cannot bear to see the child choose a different life, for the love that says mine is also the love that grieves.
The mother gives her child the whole world, then weeps that it was taken.
My sister gave up her career for her kids, and now that they have moved away she walks around the flat as if looking for something she lost.
Every time the rainbird calls in the monsoon, my mother sits at the window, waiting for my brother who works abroad, and the rain cannot wash the longing from her face.
doha with a rainbird, about a mother attached to her far away son
rainbird, mother's longing
Write a doha where a rainbird calls in the first rains and a mother waits at the window for a son who may not return, showing that the love that says mine also weeps with the sky.
The rainbird cries for the first drop, the mother for her child, and both are caught by thirst that the word mine has made.
mine, mine, my own
The word mine is the gate through which all sorrow enters the heart.
write a doha on how being possessive of people hurts us
Please write a doha about the son who cannot leave his ailing mother because he feels she is his entire world, and about how love and the hook of attachment are tangled together so tightly.
I turned down a great job in another city because I could not bear to leave my parents, and I still wonder whether that was love or something else.
A beggar outside the oil press guards his bowl as if it were all the world, and when someone nudges it, he cries as if it were his child; I'd like a doha on this.
The oil press crushes grain to give oil, but the beggar's bowl is crushed by the grip of mine.
doha with a beggar and an oil press, about being attached to what little you have
beggar, oil press, mine
Write a doha where a beggar by an oil press clutches his only bowl as if it were his entire world, showing that the hook of mine grips the poor man's heart as tightly as it grips the king's.
Every time my parents visit I count the days to their departure, and as soon as they leave I start counting the days to their return.
Meeting is a joy, parting a wound, and between them the heart that says mine swings without rest.
grief of parting
Please write a doha about the way the love between family members brings both great joy and great sorrow, because the claim of mine turns every reunion into a countdown to the next farewell.
doha about how hard it is to say goodbye to my family
Hold nothing as mine, and nothing can be taken; claim everything as mine, and everything will wound.
nothing is mine
When my mother was ill I realised that my fear came not from her illness but from the fact that I considered her mine.
doha on how saying my own makes losing things hurt more
Please write a doha about the wisdom of loving without claiming, so that when a parent, child or friend leaves, the heart is not torn, because it never held them as a possession.
